title: Arvada Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Arvada wells have a 35 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $7,800-$14,400.
h1: What Arvada Well Records Tell Rural Buyers
intro_html:
Well conditions around Arvada vary more than a single average suggests. The records include shallow wells in Denver Basin settings, fractured-bedrock wells, and permits used for domestic, monitoring, irrigation, and stock purposes. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 35 feet, while the median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for early planning, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Only 2,891 wells are recorded as constructed, 2,971 report total depth, and just 386 report pump yield. Check nearby permits, the intended use, septic layout, and access for a drilling rig before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Arvada well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
Arvada’s reported well depths are unusually spread out. The median is 35 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 137 feet. About 69% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 14% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 12% between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 1,740 feet.

That range matters when you request a drilling bid. A nearby shallow well may not predict the result on a lot with different bedrock, fractures, or elevation. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while Denver Basin aquifers appear on 99% of permits. Treat the median as a starting point, not a promised completion depth.

sections.heading: How much water Arvada wells produce
sections.html:
The reported median pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 6.0 and 13.6 gallons per minute. About 66% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 19% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those are workable results for many household systems, but yield testing and storage still matter.

Low-producing wells are present: 6% report under 1 gallon per minute, and another 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the well yield, pumping test, and recovery information rather than relying on a neighbor’s result. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin for certain uses.

sections.heading: Water levels around Arvada: shallow recently, but records are limited
sections.html:
Among the 92 records reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 14 feet. The middle half ranges from 8 to 62 feet. That can reduce the amount of pumping lift for a shallow well, but it does not establish the water level on an untested parcel.

The decade figures do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 22 feet in the 1960s, 60 feet in the 1970s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. The recent records are shallower than the older measurements, but the small reporting set and varying locations make that a local record pattern, not proof of a region-wide rise or fall.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers working near Arvada
sections.html:
Arvada’s permit record stretches from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The busiest decade was the 1990s, with 1,738 permits. The record also includes 786 permits from the 2000s, 510 from the 2010s, and 196 from the 2020s. Permit activity does not mean every well was constructed or remains active.

The most common driller entry is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 1,368 records. Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. appears on 303, and Ground Exploration LLC appears on 257. Those names help identify local records, but a buyer should still obtain the actual well construction report, permit conditions, and current status from Colorado DWR before treating an old well as a dependable supply.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost on an Arvada lot
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot. At the reported median depth of 35 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800-$2,400. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,800-$14,400. Your bid can move outside that range if the driller has to go deeper, encounters difficult ground, needs special access, or must coordinate with a septic and building layout. Get a written scope that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical work, and any required permitting or water-rights work.

sections.heading: Arvada risks to check before closing or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. Within about 10 miles, the map shows 349 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 201 historic mine features, and 59 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not automatically mean a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review the well location, upgradient land uses, and laboratory water tests.

For a property near Fairmount, Wheat Ridge, Westminster, Applewood, Shaw Heights, or Lakeside, compare neighboring permits rather than assuming conditions match across the area. Confirm casing and grout, well construction, pump performance, and a current drinking-water test. A low-yield or dry hole can change the project budget. Septic setbacks, reserve areas, driveway access, and the drilling rig’s working room should be planned together with the house site.

sections.heading: A practical Arvada plan for buying or building
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit record for the parcel and nearby wells. Look for depth, aquifer description, construction status, yield, static water level, and the permitted use. Domestic or household wells make up 41% of the use mix, while monitoring wells also account for 41%; do not confuse a monitoring or abandoned record with a usable household supply.

Before closing, make the purchase decision contingent on reviewing the water right or permit, inspecting any existing equipment, and testing the water. For a vacant lot, have a driller and septic designer review access, expected depth, well location, and wastewater setbacks before finalizing the house plan. If the proposed use is more than ordinary household service, confirm whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights approval is required.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Arvada?
faq.a: Reported Arvada-area wells have a median depth of 35 feet, with the middle half from 22 to 137 feet. About 69% are under 100 feet, but 4% exceed 600 feet and the deepest record is 1,740 feet. Nearby geology and fractures can make one parcel’s result very different from the next.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Arvada?
faq.a: The local model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $1,800-$2,400. A finished system with the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,800-$14,400. Ask for separate line items so deeper drilling or difficult access is visible.

faq.q: How much water do Arvada wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 6.0 and 13.6 gallons per minute. About 6% produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 19% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Only 386 records report yield, so a nearby result is not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Arvada?
faq.a: A permit record does not prove drinking-water safety. The area map includes 349 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 201 historic mine features, and 59 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Have the well tested by a qualified laboratory and investigate nearby land uses, especially before relying on an existing well.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Arvada?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a steady decline. Median depth to water was 22 feet in the 1960s, 60 feet in the 1970s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. Only 92 records report static water level, so this suggests a mixed local record rather than a definitive regional trend.
